Those two were Keśava and Arjuna.
Saṃjaya said:
Both of them,
possessing auspicious marks, sat down upon that chariot after having honored the assembly of ancestors.
And in a secluded place, they conversed with one another;
with palms joined in reverence, Arjuna spoke these words.
Arjuna said:
Mounted upon both armies, with weapons raised for battle,
they stood amidst the sound of conchs, trumpets, and kettledrums, and amidst the roar of lions.
O Kṛṣṇa, that which was previously spoken by Gītā has not been grasped by me as I was distracted; therefore, tell me that knowable, immortal state.
In the previous battle, you yourself repeatedly cried out, "Cut!
Pierce! Kill! Who would rule a kingdom [if they acted thus]?
O subduer of enemies, once the two principal enemies have been slain by speech,
he shall speak again through knowledge when all enemies have been destroyed.
The Blessed One said: "O Pārtha, I shall later explain that knowledge joined with yoga, by which one is never again stained by sins in any way."
Arjuna said:
I am terrified of the destruction of my own kin, including my brothers, paternal uncles, and maternal relatives; I fear hell in this world, so please tell me what must be known.
What is knowledge, and what is the object of knowledge? What is the supreme self, and how does it come into being? How indeed is the self here, and how does it become the inner self?
Explain all of this so that they may understand it according to reality,
how I, whose self is united with yoga, do not cross over my own evil deeds.

In this terrible ocean of saṃsāra, which is turbulent with the waves of sons, wives, and enemies; filled with the shoals of fish that are kinsmen and relatives; terrifying with the crocodiles of wealth; unfathomable, difficult to traverse, and hard to cross due to great calamities—may I find a means to cross it.
For it is in this ocean of saṃsāra that the measure of the waves is found.
Like a potter's wheel struck by a mallet, one wanders swiftly through heaven and hell, experiencing pleasure and pain in their entirety.
Just as clouds come and go,
O Kṛṣṇa, so do all beings in the entire world wander through the ocean of saṃsāra.
Tell me that knowledge, O Kṛṣṇa, by which the birth of a son may occur;
tell me that knowledge, O Kṛṣṇa, by which the birth of a daughter may occur.
It is not a refuge; for it is a source of flight.
[She said:
"O Mādhava, be gracious to me, for whom I shall cause [this] to be recited."
For whomsoever that [graha] of the Lord of the World always...
Why is that? Because there is no need for deliberation regarding this secret fortress;
indeed, this [teaching] is exceedingly difficult to attain.
"May I never be bound by merits or sins.
The Blessed One said:
Come, I shall tell you that which brings happiness,
so that one is not smeared by karma, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Though it dwells eternally within the body, they do not perceive it due to their lack of awakening;
that very state is the deathless ground to be known, which is not subject to destruction.

That which, having reached it, the individual soul dissolves, and having reached it, creates again—O son of Kuntī, that immortal state is to be known. A moment (kṣaṇa) consists of two parts of an eighth of a twinkling (nimeṣa). When these [twinklings] are exhausted, it is called a moment. Two moments [make up a unit of time].
Two *tuṭis* make one *lava*, and eighteen *nimiṣas* [make one *lava*].
For those who have transcended [the lower states], the *prāṇa* [cycle] consists of sixty [such units]; that which is called *bhinnābhika* brings about the night when it has reached sixty *bhinnās*.
O Lord of Gods, for one who has become thus, there is neither death nor further emission.
Immovable and moving beings always depend upon him for their livelihood.
Exhaling and inhaling, he stands as the vital breath (prāṇa) itself.
For by him, the Lord, the universe remains pervaded from its very origin.
Having made the tongue touch the palate, it remains between the teeth.
That which is emitted by oneself is called Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
it flows repeatedly from my navel in this gross form.
Then, having made that which is both supreme and non-supreme— the imperishable pervader of its own abode—
its mark, one should remain with a single-minded and undistracted focus upon the supreme peace.
By means of that arrow being uttered, the Bindu of the supreme yogin is indeed uttered,
for as long as the Self is uttered together with all its parts.
Transcending time, this [mind] undergoes dissolution and becomes colored;
remaining there again and again, it is the single-mindedness that is the bow.
One might be liberated by it in a single moment, how much more so a person who practices it constantly!
Having realized the supreme, recite [the mantra] and cultivate the meditation on non-existence.
Just as a bee remains attached to a flower, so too does one devoted to yoga;
he who, having abandoned burning [attachments], should proceed, contemplating all states of being.
Through this sacrifice, one who possesses transcendent wisdom shall attain supreme nirvāṇa;
by the recitation of this extensive text,
the wise man shall then obtain the highest bliss.
He who knows that which is called the finding of the Veda— the supreme state—
and he who finds that [state], being a knower of the Veda, shall become one who has reached the further shore of the Veda.
The knower of reality finds the Vedas through those devoted to the Vedic scriptures;
having realized that this is the Supreme Brahman, he becomes one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
He who knows the three stations, the three measures, the three Brahmas, the three syllables,
and that which is half of a half-measure, shall become one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
But that Brahmin who knows the Vedas and is devoted to the knowledge of Brahman,
having realized the Supreme, is worthy of worship by the world.
That place where a yogi who possesses the ten powers resides becomes supreme;
even by eating there but once, one’s lineage would be sustained.
Scripture, knowledge, and the eternal should be understood through the means of comprehension;
having known them in their true essence, one should abandon the quality of goodness (sattva) without remainder.
Having known the object of knowledge, one should abandon both knowledge and the desire for it in the same way.
One should discard the book entirely, just as one discards straw after gathering grain; just as one with a torch in hand might walk away after observing the object, so too,
having observed the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should then relinquish that knowledge.
Just as there is no need for milk for one who is satiated by nectar.
Having thus understood that reality, there is no further need for the Veda;
for those ignorant of the Veda, there is no power of action through penance, sacrifice, or charity, nor by non-violence.
Yet liberation shall not be theirs; rather, there will be birth and death again and again, even after they have studied the four Vedas and the various Dharmaśāstras in many ways.
All those who do not find this sacrificial navel are considered mere cattle;
for they, deluded by the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), fail to find the Self.
Those who have wandered for a long time through thousands of various births,
even by means of horse-sacrifices, Soma-sacrifices, holy places, and equal acts of charity;
For one who knows the Supreme Self, even his seat would suffice;
like a heated [iron], that [seat] constantly consumes him, as does a man on a single-legged elephant.
Through a single act of meditation, this is equal for yogis—of this there is no doubt.
He by whom the sacrifice was performed with Agni and the others is the one who receives the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
By means of a single meditative absorption, this is equal for yogins; of this there is no doubt.
[The earth] is everywhere, and from all directions, it is pure on every side.
This is equal for all yogis, there is no doubt;
it is characterized by celibacy, self-restraint, truthfulness, and non-violence.
Through a single meditation, this is undoubtedly equal for all yogis;
they cause all things that are subject to decay to undergo coming and going.
But the yogin who knows reality, having attained the supreme state, should not emit [the vital essence];
he should neither eat excessively nor remain completely fasting.
Yoga is not accomplished for one who is dejected or agitated;
rather, it belongs to one whose body is well-stabilized and whose mind is likewise serene.
"However, for one whose source is the *nirtaya* and who is *kṣārī*, his sacrifice is successful.
The Blessed One said:
The individual soul (jīva), having itself emerged from the Self within the body situated in three ways,
resounds as the Supreme Self (paramātman) within the inner self until the end of its extraction.
Inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*) are prescribed;
these are the names for the sacrifice according to the supreme *Tridhāsāra-mata*.
Wind, fire, and likewise space as the third, along with the individual soul (jīva)—
this is declared to be the vital breath of the soul, conceived as subtle as the hundredth part of the tip of a hair.
Consisting of the form of sound, it issues forth from the vital breath into the heart and the void;
because all the limbs are filled by that, it is called *pūraka* (inhalation).
Being filled, immovable, firmly established, and abiding in its manifold forms—
because the self of beings remains thus motionless and steady, it is called *kumbhaka*.
By whom the conduct throughout the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, is pervaded— he alone, Śambhu, who is the self of all beings, is established as the one.
The *pūraka* is known as Brahmā, the *kumbhaka* is said to be Viṣṇu, and by the *recaka* is Śaṅkara; thus the threefold *dhāraṇā* is remembered.
Liberation is free from merit and demerit, having the nature of space;
it is a single form divided into three parts: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
One who is bound by innate and adventitious afflictions, arising from cessation and origination,
is not liberated merely by making a distinction regarding the principles (*tattva*).
Arjuna said:
"How can there be an obstruction of the breath that is innate (*sahaja*)?
How could it be by means of something adventitious (*āgantuka*), O Kṛṣṇa? And how does the one dissolve?
The Blessed One replied:
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
mind, intellect, and ego—by these eight indeed the Supreme is established. One who is beyond these qualities is liberated; you, however, are not beyond the self of the qualities.
Just as a seed placed in a vessel does not leave it for even a single moment,
so too, O Mother, by means of one's actions, one remains within the womb, in heaven, or in hell.
When that being is born, it becomes endowed with those very qualities.
Arjuna said:
When the body, which consists of the five elements, has been divided, those [five] go in five distinct ways;
yet they remain within the merit and demerit of the body that is now deprived of the vital breaths.
The Blessed One said:
In these very pleasant things one's own good deeds [are stored], and in unpleasant things one's evil deeds.
The eternal Brahman, situated within the midst of the meditative yogis who have cast off [all bonds],
having distinguished between merit and sin, is the five deities.
They go along with the living soul as long as it remains within the body.
The eight classes of artisans are bound by the three types of livelihoods;
they are led away by auspicious or inauspicious bonds, accompanied by praise for their wares.
Just as animals are bound in captivity by the snares of karma,
so too is liberation established when one releases the self from that [bondage].
This is your [path] of restraint through the suppression of speech and the senses;
yet when all these are aroused and scattered, they merely indulge in pleasure.
Even those adventitious snares consisting of greed and anger,
when scattered by sensual passion, truly destroy the body of one who is enveloped in delusion.
Thus, bound by these three kinds of fetters, living beings are led astray;
they wander through many births, experiencing both auspicious and inauspicious states.
But the yogi who perceives the self as the supreme state shatters the single bond, just as a fierce wind disperses a dense fire.
Arjuna said:
How indeed does the Āṣā-gata move? By what means does it proceed? Its various places of arising are such that it abides in those very places here.
Having repeatedly performed inhalation and exhalation for living beings,
once it has emerged from its own body, does it enter back in again?
To what place does it go there, and from what does it return?
Tell me: is it for its own sake, for the sake of another, or for both?
He wanders alone, yet [is he] also...?
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to explain this doubt of mine to me in its entirety.
The Blessed One said:
Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth state (turya), and likewise that which is beyond; or rather, what is the fourth like? These six states belong to the Supreme by its own nature.
One should designate the waking state as being in the region of the heart, the dream state in the throat,
deep sleep in the eyes, and the fourth state (turya) as situated in the head.
The fourth state, however, is indeed beyond the tip of the nose;
thus the Self always abides within the movement of the yogis.
Brahmā resides in the waking state, Viṣṇu is always present in the dream state,
Rudra is situated in the deep sleep states, and Īśvara abides in the fourth state (turya).
Sadāśiva, however, exists at the end of the fourth state; beyond that is Paraśiva.
Having emerged by means of the self, he does not enter again.
Together with the eight full [kalās], he goes entirely along with the parts;
having abandoned the body, he indeed enters the Self through the manifestation of immortality.
Let his side come to you; indeed, come back to yourself. O Mother, let him go to the sacrifice so that he may be released from all bonds for the sake of his life-breaths.
Not knowing [this], one is cooked for a long time in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
As long as this [mind], which has sound and other qualities as its head,
is not released, it will again be bound by those [fetters] and roasted for many ages in saṃsāra.
Sound and touch go to Brahmā as their own root;
form, taste, and mind likewise attain the state of Viṣṇu.
Egoity, sound, and the state of dissolution merge into the mixture;
that which is merged into the higher and lower goes to the stream of nectar.
Absorbed in inhalation and retention, one should touch the state of the "Kumbha" (the vase); even through exhalation, reaching the limit of the other, one gives rise to the state free from disease.
Just as milk poured into milk, or ghee into ghee,
becomes indistinguishable, so too does this [individual self] become one with the Supreme Self within the self.
Having abandoned the group of eight qualities, one who is liberated from bonds goes to the Supreme.
Joy is likewise ordained;
they are liberated by mere knowledge—how much more so through sacrifice and meditative concentration!
There is nothing higher than that which is imperishable, as declared by the Vedas.
At that very moment, all [sins] such as the killing of a Brahmin are blown away by the winds;
indeed, at the instant of union, one is freed from both one's own merit and demerit.
Arjuna said:
That supreme and most difficult-to-attain knowledge of Brahman which was spoken by you,
[and] the formless fifth consciousness...?
"O Madhusūdana, tell me something of the signs that arise here day after day for the yogi who is constantly engaged in the yoga of meditation."
The Blessed One said:
The knowledge of the *tulāpuruṣa*, the entering of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*),
the practice of throwing stones from a mountain, and likewise the vision of light—
any one of these eight signs (*pratyaya*) leads to accomplishment in the supreme vision.
That perfection is to be known as supreme through direct perception;
moreover, yogis cause it to blaze forth even without [prior] knowledge.
The great manifestation of the being is the great blazing of fire;
through the true nature of the withdrawal of seeds, it destroys that which was previously established.
In the same manner, let them be withdrawn so that it becomes even more subtle.
Intellect, mind, ego, and the [subtle elements] beginning with sound and ending with form— these are the objects of meditation.
Or else, having entered the body of the deceased through the dissolution of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) consisting of taste and smell,
one should enter the abode of another's body.
Having performed the command for movement, turn back quickly;
O you who are well-deluded, [attain] steady intellect through the knowledge of Brahman for the sake of Brahman.
The white [vital breath] indeed enters its own city again through the navel of the tawny one;
the entry and likewise the exit should be performed with supreme ambrosia.
If he should ever delay for a moment and go to another's city, he will become like a kinsman; therefore, one should bring him back quickly.
Having formed the *ghaṭikā* mudrā at Prayāga, one should not cover the surface of the tongue;
by this very method, one immediately becomes [accomplished], without a doubt.
Death occurs according to one's own will; it does not come under the power of time.
For the yogin, there is freedom of choice regarding both the future and the past.
Go to the state of supreme peace through liberation from all bonds.
When the yoga of the yogins is completed, whether one is restrained or even merely touches [it], for whom there is the arising of... [the fruit].
Likewise, showing [the breath] at the tip of the nose equal to Viṣṇu at night, one indeed becomes endowed with faith; thus one should practice the fire-element concentration (āgneyādhāraṇā).
For the yogin, however, [the presence of] Viṣṇu-knowledge at the tip of the nose—[even one] joined with great sins—is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
For yogins, there is neither exhalation nor inhalation in the middle [state] of retention;
in the state of intense joy, the fire, cast forth from within, shines outwardly.
Thus, by practicing with moderate faith, one shall attain the supreme; within a year, one should practice the perfected retention of the fire-mantra (*āgneyī-dhāraṇā*).
Of those mountain minerals whose grain-nature is being burned by fire, what is done and what is not done? Through the fault of burning them, they burn away the vital breaths.
Having performed thousands of such acts, one should subsequently become devoted to meditation.
One purifies all meditative absorption (*dhyāna*),
even after having committed individually each of the misdeeds arising from the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*) within one's own birth.
Having meditated upon the fire-element concentration (*āgneya-dhāraṇā*), one becomes like a flame;
thousands of sins, including the killing of a Brahmin and unrighteous conduct, [are destroyed].
Just as a great, fully blazing fire cannot be extinguished by streams of water.
But for the yogi who knows reality, he is not destroyed by those of high or low caste;
just as one who has not been consecrated with mantras does not survive after consuming poison.
Likewise, one who knows Brahman never dwells in hell due to evil deeds.

If one were to sink into that unfathomable [ocean], what would happen? Likewise, he who eats what is not to be eaten sinks down; yet, when pierced by the principles (*tattva*), he goes to the imperishable state, just as a silkworm [is transformed] within its cocoon.
Through various actions and non-actions, he remains for many years;
meanwhile, this excellent being is restless, performing recitations, sacrifices, oblations, and the like.
O Brahmana, as long as one does not find the gift, study, and the sacred ford,
he who knows the Supreme Brahman becomes all-pervading.
In other births, one wanders through various pleasures and pains;
but having known the single-syllabled Brahman, which is devoid of even a trace of duality, [one is liberated].
Practice [this] among all castes, but do not discriminate regarding food;
one will not be smeared by sin, nor indeed will one be smeared by merit.
He goes to that state free from ailment which is the falling away of the body;
indeed, there is a distinction of caste only so long as one does not find Brahman.
Having realized the supreme Brahman,
those twice-born ones of excellent character remember it through knowledge, [relying] on their teachers, brothers, and kinsmen.
But what of those who destroy their thoughts, or dwell in the forest, or [practice] dwelling...?
By the power of the knowledge of Brahman and by the strength joined with sacrifice,
those who are liberated from both merit and sin attain the supreme goal.
Out of affection for you, I have told this supreme secret:
the Self is indeed attained by oneself through knowledge alone.
If one performs the recitation with knowledge, it is indeed attained; but if not with knowledge, it is not attained at all.
O Bhārata, even if ten thousand, a thousand,
or likewise hundreds of minds are directed elsewhere, and the eye is fixed on something else,
nevertheless, the yoga of the yogins proceeds [unimpeded].
Arjuna, with a mind focused on nothing else, should recite this reality (*tattva*) repeatedly.
For the wise, this recitation is the liberation from the snare of the limbs [of worldly existence].
With a steady intellect and free from delusion, he [realizes] Brahman... [text fragment].
Having bathed and become pure, one who is devoted to vows and restraints should perform the silent recitation (japa).
All that existence has been made equal by means of knowledge; hear now, in brief, the characteristic of the sacrifice which brings about peace.
Having attained it by themselves, they are liberated from all dualities by the best of the twice-born;
likewise, there are breath control (prāṇāyāma), meditation (dhyāna), and supreme concentration (dhāraṇā).
"By means of releasing and attracting, one should lead [the breath]; this is called the sixth. These sixfold sacrifices are remembered by the sages as bestowing liberation."
Falsehood, base vessels, anger, delusion, violence, atheism, and even pleasure— these are never, in any way, for the benefit of men.
Arjuna said:
Today my birth has become fruitful;
I have attained liberation through the discernment of reality.
Thus released, he fell upon the ground like a staff;
with palms joined in reverence, he prostrated at his feet and paid him homage.
One should proceed with equanimity toward sounds; tell me the practice of the vow.
A celibate student (*brahmacārī*) [observes] the vow... [text missing].

Constantly devoted to the field (*kṣetra*) and intent upon recitation (*japa*) and fire-offerings (*homa*), do not set out [elsewhere]; O Vasvāna, protect us from the state of being consumed by the flames of misfortune.
May there be prosperity in the four [directions].
Having attained it, O twice-born one, they are liberated from all pairs of opposites.
Having fed a Brahmin according to one's ability, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and speak of the Agnihotra sacrifice, truth, and so forth.
"It has been renounced by me; it has been renounced by me; it has been renounced by me."
Having abandoned thirst and being free from craving, he wanders along the Yamunā after granting fearlessness to all beings;
for it is said that fearlessness toward those who have been well-restrained belongs to one who possesses nails [of self-control].
O twice-born one, seeing that [the sun] has set, he moves from his place.
Even the moon trembles and becomes despondent;
so too do the gods, daityas, siddhas, and sages declare.
And those who previously went to any of the Uduṃbara hells for him.
One should cease at that very moment from conversing with him;
listen, for by uttering the syllable "va," one is liberated from all sins.
Having reached the fourth stage of life (*āśrama*), one should go forth with devotion and bow down.
He who,
having seated the most excellent and pure Vaiśya on a seat covered with grass, performs the sweeping,
sprinkling, and smearing [of the ground], obtains the fruit of the gift of Kapilā cows along with the merit of learning.
A person who, having approached with humility, offers food to ascetics together with their names,
obtains the fruit of a year’s performance of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Free from anger and harshness, without deceit and not backbiting, upright in all things— tell me everything about those among whom you dwell.
A celibate student, pure, self-controlled, of clean conduct, and ever devoted.
O Vaiśya, you have praised me with all [your might], even as you remain blind.
In a solitary place, always for a very long time,
one should recite [the mantra] until it is stainless and free from faults, as much as one desires.
Having reached a secluded place and being constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation, becoming absorbed in that very [reality], one should meditate in solitude;
thus liberated in conduct, one is intent upon vows and observances.
They go [to their respective states].
The cessation of desire and greed... [is attained]. One should consider that which is empty, hateful, and renounced as being such.
The Brahmin woman is my mother; the Kṣatriya woman is my sister; the Śūdra woman is my daughter-in-law;
and the Vaiśya woman, whose limbs are smeared with the impurities of many men, must be avoided.

Where there is the neglect of one's own duty, where there is a lack of regard for the world, where there is excessive pride, where other devotees are present, and where slander prevails— [in such places, one should not dwell].
A single ascetic excels over thousands of Brahmins.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Svara—[along with] Pra... and Sva...—I meditate upon together with the others.
They all attain satisfaction for fifteen years, just as there is a difference between the sun and a mustard seed, or between Mount Meru and a mustard seed.
...let them enter. ... [The duties] of a householder during the time of eating.
Therefore, at a śrāddha, on special occasions, on meritorious days, and on festival days...
"Whatever is to be given to me from the six directions must be given to the ascetics so that it may be imperishable.
"O Arjuna, wherever there is a monk, there I shall manifest my presence. When I am worshipped, I am indeed worshipped; when I am worshipped, all the deities are worshipped."
Even an outcaste who is my devotee, O Goddess, is a partaker of the fourth quarter of my dharma; of this there is no doubt.
How much more so those devoted to me who hate my linga? They should be known as mere dry wood; their pride is indeed due to the egoism that has arisen within you.
Those who are consumed by the fire of false views and improper paths go to the human realm of hell;
however, those who are my devotees—steadfast, born of noble families, and virtuous—go to my own world.
Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, Brahmā, the Viśvedevas, and even the Pitṛs—
having reached his mouth, [they are satisfied]. By eating it even once, O Nārada, it becomes ten million times more meritorious than all else.
How much more so when many have eaten; among them, no number can be found.

The worship of ascetics [is] for the sake of [attaining] all the gods; indeed, for those who have pride, [the worship] of all the gods is for the sake of pride. One should offer a seat, a bed, a vehicle, and whatever else the ascetic desires.
Those fools who, being deficient in conduct, hate the twice-born who possess the fourfold life-force.
Those who are devoted to other deities and hold wrong views [are] corrupting the primordial Dharma;
they defile this meritorious primordial Dharma, which is superior to all others.
How is it that those who are deluded strike down Viṣṇu himself, who is present before them?
Having seen [the consequences], those who follow evil paths go to that state of darkness in the next world;
for they are born deaf and mute from birth after birth.
One should divide his evil deed according to what is being proclaimed.
"In anger, on inauspicious days,
and [during] my impurity—
[these lead] to the destruction [of merit]," said Kārttikeya.
O Lord, you have thoroughly understood the supreme determination regarding the swans;
therefore, I wish to hear it—please explain it.
What is the characteristic of a horse as it has been described?
What are its names, such as "praṇakṣa"? And what is its form and its movement?
O Lord of Gods, what is its pervasion, and what indeed is its body? Please explain everything according to the proper method out of your grace.
Maheśvara said:

The power of moving through the sky (*khecarī*), the perfection of the sword (*khaḍgasiddhi*), the subterranean realm (*pātāla*), the sandals (*pāduka*), invisibility (*antardhāna*), and the divine eye (*cakṣus*)— all these, as well as the qualities such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest, O *Haṃsa*, are not accomplished in one place alone.
Mantras are not devoid of the *haṃsa*, nor are they bereft of Śakti and Śiva.
They do not remain without a protector, like [the elements] without wind;
nor does fire ever blaze without smoke.
In that same way, O Six-faced One, mantras do not succeed without the *haṃsa*.
Thus, in all mantras, the *haṃsa* is situated as the pervasive essence.
Devoid of that reality, they do not succeed even through hundreds of millions of recitations.
Within that [space], all [the elements] are situated;
likewise, Kālarudra, who abides in the seven [elements] beginning with wind and fire, is pierced through.
For this power flows forth, driving the autonomous machine;
once it has been pierced, [the goal] is attained.
O giver of all, cast me quickly into the fire even for a moment.
Yayāti was always satisfied even without sacrifices;
from the cowherds in the courtyards to the children and the barbarians who speak their respective tongues,
as well as the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Daityas, and others such as the Kimpuruṣas, [all were content].
She is also liberated among the ṛṣis, apsarases, yakṣīs, and rākṣasīs; likewise among the bhūtas, avatāras, yoginīs, guhyakas, mātṛkās, and so forth.
Everyone repeatedly chants "Haṃsa,
Haṃsa," yet those fools do not recognize that [Self] which resides within the body as the machine.
For so long they wander in saṃsāra, which is terrible in form and full of great fear.
O Skanda, as long as this [mantra], which consists of all reality, has not fallen [upon me] with grace, I have been afflicted; now, impelled by my devotion, it has been bestowed by me.
O Swan, they find the supreme Śiva, who is all-pervading and all-encompassing,
just as one finds the finest clarified butter when it has been extracted from curdled milk.
Thus, having scrutinized all the scriptures,
Sadāśiva extracted this supreme, divine knowledge, the highest *haṃsa*.
One should know that the stream of the Ganges' current is established within all bodies, beginning with those who have not yet performed their duties; it is the delightful Śiva.
Established in its own nature, well-settled in supreme nirvāṇa, consisting of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*),
resembling a pure crystal— this is to be known as the supreme-non-supreme (*parāpara*).
Inexpressible, incomparable, and uninterrupted on all sides,
the supreme swan of perfect nirvāṇa is the awakener of all reality.
I shall explain its extraction; listen, O Six-faced One, according to the truth:
it is the fourth seed-syllable of the second of the pervasive ones, which is supreme.
The seed-syllable of nectar is declared to be joined with sixteen digits;
it is carried on the right wing, accompanied by the Suṣumnā.
The Haṃsa, whose essence is the union of practice and the five-syllabled mantra,
sports with its creative power (kalā) throughout the two fortnights of the month of Māgha.
They say the three dots are the eye, and the mouth is proclaimed to be the resonance (nāda).
That Rudra resides within his two ears as the auspicious [state];
he is this supreme Haṃsa, the cause of all causes.
The Praṇava is the soul of all, the vital breath, the all-pervading Great Lord;
it is the creator of all, the seer of all, the omniscient, the omnipresent, and the eternal.
The self-doctor, the great sacrificer; Tārakā and Bhinnatārakā; the ancient one of old; the maker of seals (mudrāyaḥ); he who is well-known as Purandara;
Vāsava, Avasava, and Vāsā; Hāṣa; the one of great creative power among the gods.
O Kṣattrajña, it is proclaimed as the Praṇava, the Jīva, the "I," and Sākṣin.
Mahākāla, possessed of splendor, great strength, and valor;
of great heroism, a great swan, and bearing the form of Mahābhairava.
The great gift, the great sacrifice, the great accomplishment, the initiator—
this is the determination of the *haṃsa*.
Oṃ, homage to Mahābhairava!
On the peak of Mount Kailāsa, in the forest frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
crowded with perfected yogis and endowed with various trees.
It was crowded with hosts of apsarases, frequented by yakṣas and gandharvas,
filled with various [beings], and variegated with its own elemental constituents.
It was strewn with many peaks, frequented by hosts of Gaṇas and Gandharvas,
endowed with a thousand rays, and possessed the luster of molten gold.
It was frequented by ṛṣis and hosts of siddhas,
with its interior forests of karṇikāra trees in bloom along with campaka and other blossoms.
Adorned with *sarja*, *arjuna*, *kadamba*, and *pāṭalī* trees,
he stayed there on that delightful mountain together with her.
It was studded with various sounds upon a golden throne,
adorned with a garland of skulls and beautified by the divine *kuñca* ornament.
He is endowed with sixteen arms and twelve eyes; he wears a crown of matted hair and has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
He was like a blazing fire, most terrible;
he wore a serpent as a sacred thread, and possessed large nostrils and earrings.
The God of gods shines resplendent upon the girdle of the lord of serpent kings, his waist filled with jeweled threads, as he bears Umā as half of his own body.
O God, [he is] terrifying with a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and a trident (śūla) in hand;
he holds a spear (śakti) and an axe (paraśu), adorned with a rosary (akṣamālā); in his great hand he holds a vessel, well-fashioned at the rim and encircled.
Clad in a tiger skin, he was difficult even for the gods to behold.
Koṭarākṣa-Mahāśambhu, adorned with great [ornaments],
licking with his great tongue, is the creator of the world and the originator of creation.
The skull-cup is held in the left hand, and likewise the hand holds the *ḍamaruka* drum; furthermore, there are many other attributes such as the discus, the bow, the sword, and so forth.
Pa * haṃsa? and likewise the creator of emanations, the Bhaṭṭārakaṅkara;
laughing, shouting "kilakila," and bearing a most terrifying laugh.
Having assumed a terrifying form and surrounded by great yogins,
he thus [attains] the nectar of Kālaka’s bliss.
Just as a young girl finds no pleasure in the presence of a fool,
so too does a man who knows only evil turn his back upon Kālaka.
Thus, those deluded by ignorance are not confounded by the web of scriptures;
they do not know the supreme bliss, for they possess the knowledge of the Kula and the supreme nectar.
O Goddess, the power of will (icchā-śakti) presides over the attainment of whatever is desired;
by whatever form or by whatever vow one may approach [the deity].
Where there is no mark of the serpent's coil through the desire for duality or non-duality,
that which I speak on the proper occasion is like the sacrificial pap (caru).
Whether a householder, a student, one who does not dwell in a fixed abode, or one possessing form—
whether acting according to his desire or staying wherever he may be.
In whatever way it may be, O Goddess, even that which is endowed with the weightiest of gurus and equal to the power of Rudra— that Kali who [remains] does not attain success.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Timirodghāṭana*.
Bhairava said:
In the world, one may speak of the meaning of the scriptures in one way while acting otherwise;
yet those who are satisfied with the nature of the syllables and contemplate the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras do not perceive the supreme peace,
being deluded though they are scholars of worldly affairs.
How could he possess knowledge even through hundreds of millions of books?
[To him] camphor, saffron, and the like are as useless as water carried by a donkey.
Those who have been deluded by discarding the many accomplishments attained through discipline do not find the supreme bliss of the Kaula, O fair-faced one.
Those who find satisfaction in the mantra-tantras, whose conviction is based on mere ritual consumption,
and those humble men who remain content without having attained the Kaulika knowledge.
White, yellow, and so forth are perceived in others; likewise, pungent and other tastes, as well as circular forms such as earrings, are perceived through the nourishment by fire.
Such as these, and likewise others, are the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), as well as the supreme [purification],
the subtle [purification] of the bindu and nāda, and indeed one's own path (*svādhvāna*).
Having known the reality of knowledge and the ritual procedure, those men devoted to Śiva who are dissatisfied [with worldly things] should,
by means of their own self, destroy all obstacles through the Kaulika [path] and the auspicious Bhaginīs.
The sacrificial post for the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices may be made either of gold or of clay.
O Goddess, according to such a view, there is no Kaula whatsoever even for anyone;
[it is like] searching for the supreme moon in the sky, or like a six-tusked elephant.
Thus he spoke as Kaulīśa wandered upon the surface of the earth,
[the mantra] joined with the syllable *rañji* and endowed with the syllables of the Kaula-vidyā.
O Mahādeva, how can the sacrifice of the wish-fulfilling jewel of meditation occur within the inconceivable body? This is my doubt; please explain this with your own voice.
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, that which is the heart of all embodied beings,
when awakened by the flowing stream of the source of knowledge, becomes purified.
O Goddess, that which exists as the pervasive form where Śiva and Śakti are united—this is the power of Rudra; its immersion resides within the mouth of the Guru.
That which they call the inconceivable, the final, auspicious, and supreme cause— from that has emerged His power (śakti), which differentiates between sound (nāda) and the point (bindu).
And as soon as that has been performed, the signs arise;
even for one who is emaciated, a stabilization of the *piṇḍa* is produced.
O Goddess, in that divine practice, the divine [state] is situated there;
O Goddess, one has a vision of her together with the three Yoginīs.
Of whom? Of that divine one, O fair-faced goddess, who dwells even among the gods;
for as is the practice, O Goddess, so does creation proceed.
First the heart trembles, then the palate rises, and the head whirls; this is the characteristic sign of the transition into emanation (*sṛṣṭisaṃkrānti*).
One should rotate the body one by one through the joints of the limbs and sub-limbs;
by the power of the Kaula-vidyā, this entire body becomes whirled.
(30) * * * By her own will, she assumes various states; in each of those, the Supreme Goddess sports as she pleases.
Nor is one afflicted by ghosts, demons, or the darkness [of ignorance],
nor is one released from suffering through anything contrary [to the Dharma].
In the form of the power of will (icchā-śakti), she becomes the Guru for the yogi;
she is the supreme one who brings the bliss of passion to the body and removes all sins.
Those whose minds are relished by sacrifice undergo the transition from being dear to being disliked, [casting aside] their sons, friends, wives, and accumulation of wealth.
And the gods, stationed in their celestial chariots, behold him, O fair-faced one,
whose consciousness has been subdued by the mantra and tantra.
The immersion into the power of Rudra is a constant, unconscious absorption;
through union with the divine deities, it is the cause of supreme bliss.
The cosmic egg bestows the fruit of worldly enjoyment;
the immersion into the power of Rudra arises within the perceptions of sound.
O fair-faced one, being constantly engaged in yoga, he does not distinguish between day and night;
he knows neither hunger nor thirst, nor indeed any great affliction.
It produces joy, contentment, and the bliss of the true Self;
when joined with consciousness, it performs manifold mudrā-bindings.

It causes trembling, singing, dancing, and various other transformations; through the alteration of the impurities, it produces many kinds of states, both those caused by others and those produced by oneself.
And it shakes off the mass of impurities; established in the supreme [state], if what has been spoken were unreal, then the world would not proceed at all.
The sign of yoga is not seen, nor is any knowledge found to be deluded anywhere;
if it were to be deluded for him, then it is certain that it belongs to someone else.
Otherwise, why would it not proceed in this way even through millions of treatises?
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Timirodghāṭana*.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess: there is no Kaula [teaching] above or below, nor is it based on instruction.
When knowledge has been transmitted, then liberation is certain.
The cage of the body revolves like a potter's wheel bound by the Kula.
The Creator partakes of that which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Attraction, subjugation, inciting enmity, eradication, and killing; as well as the facing of kings, paralyzing, immobilizing, and so forth.
She produces conviction, destroys obstacles, and bestows manifold accomplishments;
she also grants the vidyās that are proclaimed in the mantras and tantras.
That Karmāṣṭa is fully perfected, bestowing the fruits of all actions;
it is the ultimate of all tantras, differentiated among all castes.
The *mṛtasaṃjīvanī* [mantra] is for reviving the dead; it is beautiful when drawn with vermilion. It is known to be yellowish-white for paralyzing and effective for the seventh [rite], *uccāṭana*.
Black in color, she brings death to enemies in battle; red-hued, she shines with the splendor of a lotus through her beauty, grace, and majesty. She is the very embodiment of liberation.
Aṇimā, laghimā, mahimā, and prāpti;
prākāmya, the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), vaśitva, and yatra-kāmāvasāyitā.
The eighth is proclaimed as being far beyond hearing and seeing;
through the power of the Kaula Vidyā, the eightfold qualities of sovereignty shall arise.
I shall now relate that which is dear to you, by means of which virtues arise.
And these twelve [verses], which are the essence of all the Mārṣas, must be guarded with great effort; the scribe should not write them down.
Or twelve verses, O fair-faced one, in seven days.
It is not given to one who merely recites; it should be transmitted from ear to ear.
Having obtained that, there will be accomplishment in existence—the equal flavor of the emission of the *ūrṅkara*.
At that very moment, O lady, your mudrā is undoubtedly Khecarī;
the seed-syllable consists of a single creation, and Rudrā is indeed the singular Khecarī.
These two are to be known as the eyes of the method; one who stands on the ground of blindness cannot see, but he who is established in that state can reveal even the three worlds through sacrifice.
O Lord, what could possibly arise at that very moment of its birth?
Thus ends the fifth chapter, "The Dispelling of Darkness. 5.
The Goddess said:
When it migrates to the lungs, it displays signs such as a spear;
established within the body, it produces those true and manifest effects.

How is it that she who is to be known as having transmigrated is described as one who has not transmigrated? And how is she whose jewels have not been stepped upon; why does she not go upward by half?
O Supreme Lord, tell me what the signs of one who has attained perfection are.
Bhairava said:
She who pervades the universe, including all things mobile and immobile, by means of her all-pervading form,
extending both horizontally and vertically— she is remembered as the All-Pervasive One (Sarvavyāpinī).
She resides within the internal and external body, present in all living beings; she is always in the region of the True Teacher, yet she transfers into the bodies of others.
The characteristic of the transference of the body consists of its stationary state and its movement upward and downward;
O fair-faced one, the downward movement is characterized by withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), while the upward movement is creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
The movement of stability proceeds through the threefold sacrifice. (p.
32) In this manner, it should be pierced sequentially by means of the single [reality] that begins with the three.
One should cause the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) to enter, pervading the body from top to bottom;
he who possesses these signs is known as a Guru who bestows grace.
Having performed all the ritual services with one's own person or wealth,
that supreme consciousness which resides within the mouth of the Guru should be received.
With the jewel of the Kaula instruction, the yogi should behold the divine vision with eyes closed, and then behold it again through direct perception.
The Yoginī first appears as a mere shadow again and again;
in whatever way one practices yoga, in that very form she manifests.
"Behold her! Whether in the form of Kṛṣṇa, or as Raudrī, or with a gentle form; adorned with various ornaments, she remains both visible and invisible, moving about in manifold forms."
Constantly stationed in the intermediate space, they all behold the Mother,
who appears in the form of Raudra-Bhairava and is surrounded by many yogis.
O fair-faced one, when the Kaulika yoga has been attained through existence, he, the Lord of Yoga, beholds his very self as the Supreme.
Having abandoned that substance which exists upon the earth and would lead one to liberation, one should not speak falsely to the Guru who bestows the Kaula instruction and grants liberation.
But for one who has renounced worldly existence from the very heart, this [gift] is not to be given.
The divine nectar of the Kaula knowledge resides within all beings;
I have described only a small portion of it, though it is found within tens of millions of divisions.
Success in Khecarī is said to be attained within twenty-seven years;
the lord of yogis who is constantly devoted to this practice succeeds very quickly indeed.
Thus, O beloved, everything that was asked by her has been explained.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Timirodghāṭana*.
The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, you have related the very extensive yoga of the Kaula;
having seen the forms in their proper sequence, how does liberation come to be?
Bhairava said:
The lord of yogis, ever-perpetually disciplined, beholds the entire triple world;
he perceives the cosmic egg as distinct [from himself], and his day passes as he attains Śiva.
In the beginning, one sees forms even when the eyes are closed at the end of a dream;
through the yoga of constant practice, there is the direct perception of the deity.
Even by means of speech he hears them, or by their touches, or even their scents;
for the Lord of Yogis, whose mind is established in truth, possesses overwhelming power.
Assuming a divine form, I shall display myself in the sky before all the world;
I shall perform many wonders, acting according to my own will as I desire.
But joined with the meaning of the scriptures and united with the Vedānta,
he composes a graceful poem, charming and adorned with poetic figures.
They agitate the entire world, which is colored by their enchanting conduct;
they possess the power to enter both women and men, and their song is truly captivating.
The yogi perceives himself as established in divine yoga,
as well as the goddess in Pātāla, in the world of the Nāgas, and throughout the three worlds.
There were various human beings, as well as trees, shrubs, and creepers;
bipeds and quadrupeds, and many kinds of aquatic creatures.
He should cause various delightful provincial districts, villages, and cities,
as well as diverse syllables, to appear in the sky.
Other islands, oceans, rivers, groves, and mountains;
birds of various forms, and especially dogs—[all these appear] within the dream-vision.
He beholds the celestial chariots of the moon and sun, the world of Indra,
the delightful city of the Guardians of the Quarters, as well as the cities of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
He who sets in motion activity throughout the celestial, human,
and subterranean realms manifests his supreme power over the three worlds, including all that is moving and stationary.
The city of Rudra is together with the five-faced one, filled with Śiva;
it is Sadāśiva, the supreme, presided over by Parāśakti.
Above that, Śiva, peaceful and established without interruption,
transcends the power of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa-śakti*) and reaches the supreme state.
Beyond the sky, O Goddess, they attain the peace that is both supreme and non-supreme liberation;
this has been told to you in due order, O Goddess, as the supreme and the non-supreme.
O Goddess, one established in the Kaula sacrifice shall quickly attain the state of peace.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Timirodghāṭana*.
The Goddess said:
Devoid of the syllables of mantra and vidyā, and lacking meditative concentration and retention,
how can knowledge be understood as that which is taught by the Five Jewels?
Bhairava said:
The Kaula descent of creation, characterized by the meaning of the supreme texts,
is obtained through the instruction of Rudra’s power within the mouths of the gurus.
All mantra-tantras, the deities,
and the discourses on ritual procedures do not succeed, even if they are great, for one who is devoid of the power of Rudra.
The heart is known as the supreme vitality of all vidyās and mantras;
he who does not know the immersion into the power of Rudra does not attain success.
The painting is the Kaula knowledge, which resides within the mouths of the gurus;
it is transmitted from ear to ear, for indeed, one who stands at a distance cannot receive it.
One should cause the knowledge of meditation and concentration, the instruction on *yoganāda*,
the instructions on the five jewels, and the meaning of the texts to be written down.
When the first jewel is attained through practice, there is the destruction of gray hair;
thereafter, his body blazes upward, and he proceeds to the supreme state.
By the power of the second jewel, the Guru was pleased by his disciple;
honored by the circle of Yoginīs, they remained established here and there.
Thirdly, when the power (śakti) has transferred into one's own body from the body of another,
the one of great strength, established in samādhi, agitates all the cities [of the senses] before him.
Having attained the fourth, the siddhi of Bhūcarī, one goes forth;
then, having bound the fifth, Khecarī Mudrā, one goes upwards.
Having gone before Maheśvarī, Umā proceeds once again;
having meditated upon the state beyond the mind (manonmanī), she enters a contemplation that occurs unexpectedly.
Established therein, the great yogi perceives the entire world;
through certain practice, yoga may be cultivated in a forest or even on a mountain.
Completely liberated from all dualities, the yogi quickly attains accomplishment;
beheld by the power of perfected vidyā, he produces conviction.
Loss of vision, delusion, insanity, and so forth;
likewise, those who are stout, short, tall, children, the elderly, and the young.

In the midst of the fire of the universal net (*viśvajālāgni*), one should effect the transition (*saṃkrāma*). One should paralyze [the breath] within the great bindu; and the afflictions arising from bodily obstacles are [stilled] during the transition among the animals and the stones.
One should perform the grasping with the sacrificial animal; it transforms into one's own body.
Having attained perfection through sacrifice, it sports, assuming manifold forms and cognitions.
Everything pertaining to the world and beyond, whatever has been done by whomsoever,
whatever is yet to come in the future— whether it be fear, one's own welfare, or that of others.
By the power of the Supreme Śakti, the yogi who remains established in that samādhi and is constantly devoted to yoga has no doubt regarding that time [of liberation]. || 0 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Dispelling of Darkness.
The Goddess said:
How is the supreme power (parā-śakti) arisen, and how does it pervade the three worlds? How do yogis meditate upon her, who bestows the path to liberation for all?
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, you consist of all the gods; you abide beyond all worlds;
you are all-pervading, beginningless, and worshipped among all the gods.
Pervading the fourteen worlds and situated above Brahmā,
may Śiva and Śakti [grant] all [blessings].
Seated upon the lotus posture, [he is] the maṇḍala of...;
with matted hair and a bark garment, [he is] Brahmā...
They worship him who holds the conch, discus, and mace;
he whose body is smeared with ashes, who carries a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), and who is radiant with his ornaments of skulls.
O Sulocanā, I am indeed not one who wears matted locks of hair;
rather, it is the Supreme Śakti whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara meditate upon.
She is distinct from all other objects of focus for gods, asuras, and yogins alike.
The supreme Kalā meditates upon the Lord of Devas, Indra, the Guru, and the others;
indeed, was she questioned by the city of the gods and by the mighty Dānavas? By me as well, the Śakti has been meditated upon, and everything else exactly so.
O Lord, at that very moment, the supreme power Parāśakti arrived, free from all affliction,
accompanied by hundreds of thousands, millions, tens of millions, and many crores of Yoginīs.
Though one, she exists in many forms, pervading all states;
though one, she is established within many divisions, divided by threefold distinctions.
By your grace alone, O Mother, she becomes one as soon as she is born, yet possesses great power.
The second is the intermediate power (madhyamā-śakti), which resides in the mouth of Ya;
it consists of the Vidyā, Dhyāna, and Samādhi, and is the instructor of the Yoganāda.
It effects the transmission of knowledge through immersion in the power of Rudra;
through the instruction of the Guru and practice, one attains the state beyond the senses.
Among the thirty-two wheels of the Mothers, it is the third...
For these qualities do not exist [without them], as they bestow divine vision and liberation.
The third transition of Śakti has been described as that which belongs to the Kula of the Yoginīs, by means of the entry into the true path.
He is remembered as one who has attained bliss,
having abandoned the web of reality and embraced the Kaulika meaning which is perfectly tranquil.
O Goddess, a guru is difficult to find; one who is even greater than a guru is most difficult to find.
The attainment of that very [state] is difficult to obtain; yet it has been attained by him who... For such an attainment is indeed difficult to find even in the Kaula seat through diligent effort.
Many have gone to the sacred fields and seats (*kṣetrapīṭha*) and wandered there;
yet, even after twelve years, some do not see [the truth] at all.
O Goddess of gods, even one who is well-refined and learned in the meaning of many granthas remains unsuccessful regarding the *pīṭhas* and *upapīṭhas* if he persists in delusion.
A fool who has not grasped the meaning of all the scriptures,
having obtained [it] through the Kaula seed-syllable, attains the radiant accomplishment of the three worlds.
Thus, O Goddess, this Yoga, which is supreme among the Kaulas and the most excellent conclusion of all Tantras, bestows liberation; it must be guarded again and again.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Timirodghāṭana*.
Bhairava said:
One should conceal this secret text even from one's own beloved;
it should not be given to those whose passion is not yet awakened, nor to those who revile, nor to those who are hostile.
One who is addicted to vice, one born in the forest (or a forest-dweller), one with deformed nails due to anger,
a rogue, one who is fickle and wicked, one who is base, a slanderer, and one afflicted by consumption— these are [excluded].
One afflicted by disease, a mere logician, one who neglects constant conduct and vows,
a crow-like demon, one with little learning yet full of envy, and a defiler of the rules of conduct.
One born of an outcaste, one who is violent, one with black teeth, one who has not conquered his senses,
a reviler of gurus, gods, and the twice-born, and the husband of a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*).
A performer for hire? A sage? One wounded by the sword? One intent on desire?
A Tārkṣakaṇa? A wolf of nihilism? This one is cruel, having abandoned his own duty.

One who avoids obstructing others and encroaching on their space, who abstains from prostitutes and the wives of others, who is free from the desire for sons and the attachment to begging bowls, who is pure in his acquisitions, and who has conquered anger— [such a one is liberated].
Ungrateful, with senses equanimous, tranquil in soul, and firmly attached to Śiva... or... firm.
Patient and thinking "it is conquered," for two moments...
[I am] free from envy toward all beings, as if toward my own kinsmen.
Is the Guru and Lord ever-attentive, skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures,
devoted to the teaching of Śiva,
and likewise a compassionate agent who [liberates one] from the cycle of existence?
Attached to his own small circle of friends, he is dissatisfied with himself, agitated, and greedy.

One who observes all the rules of fasting, whose self is disciplined, who is dear [to the teacher], who is virtuous, a protector of the sacred conventions (*samaya*), tranquil, with senses subdued, pure in soul, a worshiper of the Guru, of excellent character, peaceful, and free from affliction—such a Brahmin is worthy; others are not. One should not bestow [the teachings] upon those of other castes. At the three times of day, for one who is destined to exist within the five elements, [the teaching] should not be given.
However, it may be given to well-examined disciples who are guarded, firm, and intent on their welfare.
Among these castes, one should cause [the disciple] to offer property—even grass—as well as wife, sons, and so forth, for the sake of the Guru.
He who conducts himself in this manner should offer everything he possesses.
The ultimate nature of these [elements] is to be seen as equal in all directions;
the Self is the manifold seer of the supreme reality,
whether by means of substance or through Maya, and so forth once again.
They offer oblations to that very reality, yet the Self does not take pleasure in that;
rather, the one whose mind is disciplined meditates upon it for twelve or two days without weariness.
Endowed with the powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, omniscience arises;
[this occurs] through three faces with five Brahmins, or six, seven, or eight [faces] in the case of a woman.
After ten or twelve years, having been examined for excrement, urine, and the [signs of] arrows and disease, it should be given to one who is not an atheist and does not revile [the teacher].

whether he be a Brahmin who is deceitful, or even a Mleccha who is not deceitful.

O Teacher, who are equal to Śiva, show favor to the world!

But when one has attained [the goal] through greed for material wealth, as well as by kinsmen and relatives—who will then act as the teacher (*guru*) or the one who extends the thread [of the lineage]? one should inform [him] and likewise honor the teacher.

Whether in a state of composure or even while playing,

One may eat according to one's desire, O Bhāsa, and one may observe vows according to one's desire;
the sacrifice is devoid of ritual implements and is free from all formal rites.

yet it is devoid of the syllables of Tantric lore and free from the need for meditation and mental concentration.
O Goddess, that secret which is free from thought, the subtle and supreme nectar—

Those intent on the nectar-like samādhi attain liberation through practice;
practice leads to supreme yoga, and one shall touch samādhi.
One who is free from the three impurities does not perceive [it as an object];
one sees that which is situated within the body, having the form of a black bee on a Kadamba flower and possessing a brilliance equal to ten million suns.

This expansion of the Kaulika [tradition] is found within the divine vow;

How is it that this seal-less [state] is what it is? And why this astonishment?

O Tāmra, when the beloved knowledge is directly perceived within the self,
that erroneous cognition perishes once [the truth] is seen.

But in the other world as well, all [these] have come again to grant liberation;

In this way,
when the knowledge of the Guru becomes directly manifest to oneself, [one reaches] the end of all wealth.
The teacher who bestows divine instruction is as rare as a celestial deity;
for while there are many gurus there, their words are empty and lack conviction.
Some, through the omission of that [duality], are devoid of pride and ignorance.
Who are they? Those who are satisfied with mere mantras, [neglecting] the very small [practice], and those who, being base, do not honor the Preceptor in the Praṇava.

O Goddess, how could this be?
How can passion and egoism, these two enemies, exist in mutual opposition?
O fair-faced one, how can the true existence of Kaulika knowledge belong to them?
[It belongs to one who is] unattached, not joined with the supreme, and endowed with the Kula throughout the various births.

By what does this living being live, and by what path does it move?

they are called the life-force (*jīva-prāṇa*), imagined to be subtler than the hundredth part of the tip of a hair.
The soul (*jīva*) joined with purity (*sattva*) should be known as white;
that which is joined with passion (*rajas*) is proclaimed [as red];
and the soul joined with darkness (*tamas*) will certainly be black.
Endowed with the living being and the essence, they are joined together.
The earth is pervaded by the King;
one should know that it extends as far as the tip of the nose.

"Like the individual soul," it was thus stated by Śiva, the Supreme Self.

The Lord experiences the sense objects while remaining within the cavities of the mouth and nostrils.
Established within the body, the individual soul (jīva) sees, smells, hears, and experiences both the auspicious and the inauspicious; thus the jīva is situated within the body.
When living beings, having abandoned the body, have ascended into the external space,
then those living beings become free from sense-objects.
Having meditated upon that Brahmā who is unborn, new, and free from becoming, he becomes Sadāśiva;
and by constantly meditating upon Śiva, the unborn, one is liberated from the cage of sin.
Infinite and residing within all bodies, Śiva abides at the tip of the nose;
he is seen by all beings, yet he is not perceived.
O Goddess, the reality of perfection (siddhitattva), which is utterly pure, resides in the center of the navel;

And the eighth seed-syllable, known as the individual soul (jīva), resides within the body;
having emerged from the center of the navel, it remains pervading the sense objects.

just as a dry leaf is carried by the wind,
so does that which is called the "living soul" (jīva), known as the vital breath (prāṇa), wander within the body.
Joined with the vital breath and the non-vital breath, [the Self] resides within the heart like Bhīma; joined with merit and sin,
it is the inner controller who, through power, [arouses] the resonance (*nāda*).

by it all is eternally pervaded...
[of the root there is but one, yet its branches are manifold].

At the end of the stainless cause, there is the eternal, immovable form;

That reality is devoid of the six phonemes; it is the supportless support. Its nature is like a wheel-track, and its nature is the central mass.
Always practicing yoga with constant devotion, one should accomplish the supreme *piṇḍa* while joined in a single hermitage and dwelling in a single place.
There is no going to external seats (pīṭhas) or fields (kṣetras);

Wherever the excellent fire of the *vali* arises, there is that which originates from the *kula*:
the support of the *kula*, the *kula*-seat, the *akula*, and the guardian of the field (*kṣetrapālaka*).

The great sacrificial pit situated within the body is a blazing sphere of splendor,
resembling the fire of cosmic destruction and possessing a radiance equal to a flash of lightning.

then one's own kaula-nature arises, by which one attains nirvāṇa.
